query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

cited_evidence.text: In our previous work, we prepared CoxCrCuFeMnNi and CoCrxCuFeMnNi HEAPs using the MA process, studied their alloying behavior and magnetic properties, and found that some HEAPs have excellent soft magnetic properties and thermal stability [,,]. Ni is also one of the main factors affecting the alloying behavior and properties of HEAs. The increase in Ni content can inhibit the formation of the intermetallic compound phase in the HEAs and promote the formation of an FCC phase, which is conducive to improving the plasticity and corrosion resistance of the HEAs [,]. The effect of Ni on the phase structure of stable HEAPs has not been reported, especially at high temperatures. The high-temperature stability of HEAPs is very important for the microstructure and properties of sintered alloys. Therefore, in this study, a mechanical alloying method was used to prepare CoCrCuFeMnNix HEAPs, and their alloying behavior and thermal stability were emphatically studied in order to understand the effect of Ni on the microstructure of stable HEAPs, which will lay a preliminary foundation for the impact of powder superalloys on the microstructure and properties.

AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. Previous studies have shown that Ti has a negative mixing enthalpy with Co and Ni. Therefore, it is easy to alloy Ti into CoCrFeNi matrix []. Moreover, the addition of Ti is conductive in solid solution strengthening and, hence, improves the mechanical properties of HEAs [,]. Löbel et al. added Ti into AlCoCrFeNi alloy and found the hardness and wear resistance of the alloy are increased significantly, which gives it potential for surface protection applications []. Besides, the addition of Ti also enhances the corrosion resistance of AlCoCrFeNiCu alloy in the HNO3 solution. The corrosion current density of the AlCoCrFeNiCuTi is reduced by 1–2 orders of magnitude, as compared with the substrate []. However, the excessive addition of Nb, Ti, or Mo can adversely affect the corrosion resistance of the alloys [,] Therefore, there is a need for a systematic study on the effects of various amounts of Ti addition to the CoCrFeNi matrix on the corrosion resistance and mechanical properties of the CoCrFeNiTix to develop HEA systems with improved properties. decision.trend: The trend in the research is to investigate the corrosion resistance and thermal stability of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in various environments, including molten salts and aggressive salt exposure at high temperatures. The studies have shown that HEAs can exhibit improved corrosion resistance and thermal stability compared to traditional alloys, but the mechanisms behind these properties are not yet fully understood.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved problem is to understand the mechanisms behind the corrosion resistance and thermal stability of HEAs, particularly in relation to the material's microstructure, composition, and processing history. Additionally, there is a need to develop a testable mechanistic hypothesis that can explain the corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel under room- and high-temperature regimes.
decision.lever: investigate the effect of microstructure and composition on corrosion resistance and thermal stability
decision.why: This next step is necessary to understand the underlying mechanisms behind the corrosion resistance and thermal stability of HEAs, and to develop a testable mechanistic hypothesis that can explain the corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel. By investigating the effect of microstructure and composition on corrosion resistance and thermal stability, researchers can identify the key factors that influence these properties and develop strategies to optimize them.
